overview.main_topic: Loading Reuters with keras.datasets, its size, the integer-sequence representation of each newswire, decoding back to text, and integer topic labels 0-45
overview.central_idea: Reuters is packaged in Keras exactly like IMDb. With num_words=10000 each of the 8,982 training and 2,246 test newswires is a list of word indices, which can be decoded using the word index with an offset of 3. Each label is an integer topic index between 0 and 45.
overview.importance: Inspecting the raw data before modelling is a habit the book insists on. This page shows that the inputs have the same format as IMDb, so the same vectorisation can be reused, and that the labels are now integers over 46 classes. That changes how labels are encoded and which loss is used (p.142, p.148).

summary:
Like IMDb and MNIST, **Reuters comes packaged with Keras**. **Listing 4.11** imports `reuters` from `keras.datasets` and calls `reuters.load_data(num_words=10000)`, which returns `(train_data, train_labels), (test_data, test_labels)`. As with IMDb, `num_words=10000` **keeps only the 10,000 most frequent words** in the data; rarer words are dropped.

The dataset is small: **8,982 training examples** and **2,246 test examples**, as the `len()` calls show. As with IMDb, **each example is a list of integers (word indices)**. The page prints `train_data[10]`, a 31-integer sequence starting `[1, 245, 273, 207, ...]` and ending `..., 4329, 17, 12]`. The leading `1` is the start-of-sequence marker.

If you are curious, **listing 4.12** decodes a newswire back to words. It fetches `word_index = reuters.get_word_index()` (a word-to-index dictionary), inverts it into `reverse_word_index` (index to word), and joins `reverse_word_index.get(i - 3, "?")` for every index in `train_data[10]`. The callout explains the **offset of 3**: indices 0, 1 and 2 are reserved for "padding", "start of sequence" and "unknown", so a stored index *i* corresponds to word-index rank *i - 3*. Indices without a match, including those reserved ones, become `"?"`.

Finally, **each label is an integer between 0 and 45**, a topic index; `train_labels[10]` is `3`. With 46 classes, these labels will need either one-hot encoding with categorical crossentropy or sparse categorical crossentropy on the integers (the next pages and p.148).

concepts.name: Reuters newswire dataset
concepts.definition: Short newswires published by Reuters in 1986, labelled with 46 topics; in Keras, 8,982 training and 2,246 test examples, each a list of word indices, with integer labels 0-45.
concepts.intuition: A pile of short wire-service news items, each filed under exactly one subject heading.
concepts.technical: reuters.load_data(num_words=10000) returns NumPy object arrays of variable-length int lists and int label arrays. Index 1 marks the start of the sequence; word index ranks are shifted by 3.
concepts.significance: The book's first multiclass problem; small enough to train in seconds on a CPU.
concepts.misconception: The 46 topics are not evenly represented; accuracy should be judged against a baseline (p.147).

concepts.name: Word-index encoding with reserved indices
concepts.definition: Each word is replaced by an integer rank; indices 0, 1 and 2 are reserved for padding, start-of-sequence and unknown, so stored indices are shifted by 3 relative to get_word_index().
concepts.intuition: Seat numbers in a theatre where the first three seats are always kept for staff.
concepts.technical: Stored index = word_index[word] + 3. Decoding computes reverse_word_index.get(i - 3, "?"). For i in {0, 1, 2}, i - 3 is negative and matches no word, so these become '?'.
concepts.significance: Needed to convert between text and model inputs. The same convention appears for IMDb.
concepts.example: The first token 1 decodes to '?' (start of sequence). The token 245 decodes to the word whose rank is 242.
concepts.misconception: Forgetting the offset gives a fluent-looking but completely wrong decoded text.

concepts.name: Integer class labels
concepts.definition: Targets given as category ids, here integers between 0 and 45.
concepts.intuition: Labels on drawers: their numbers are names, not measurements.
concepts.technical: To train a 46-way softmax you either convert them to one-hot vectors of length 46 (categorical_crossentropy) or keep them as integers with sparse_categorical_crossentropy; both compute the same loss.
concepts.significance: It decides the label preprocessing and the loss.
concepts.misconception: Treating the topic ids as numbers to regress on would impose a meaningless order on the topics.

code.title: Loading the Reuters dataset
code.original_code:
from keras.datasets import reuters

(train_data, train_labels), (test_data, test_labels) = reuters.load_data(
    num_words=10000
)
code.what_it_does: Downloads (the first time) and loads the Reuters train/test splits, keeping only the 10,000 most frequent words.

line_explanations.explanation: Imports the Reuters dataset module from keras.datasets.
load_data returns two tuples, (train_data, train_labels) and (test_data, test_labels); num_words=10000 drops words outside the top 10,000.

code.inputs_outputs: Output: train_data (8,982 lists of ints), train_labels (8,982 ints in 0-45), test_data (2,246 lists), test_labels (2,246 ints).
code.algorithm: Fetch the cached file, filter word indices by frequency rank, split into train/test.
code.theory_link: Capping the vocabulary fixes the input dimensionality used by the multi-hot vectorisation.

parameters.name: num_words=10000
parameters.role: Size of the vocabulary kept: the 10,000 most frequent words.

pitfalls: The data arrays contain Python lists of varying length; they cannot be fed to a Dense layer until vectorised (p.142).

code.title: Number of training and test examples
code.what_it_does: Shows the dataset sizes: 8,982 training and 2,246 test newswires.

line_explanations.explanation: 2,246 test samples, about 20% of the 11,228 total.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: the arrays from listing 4.11. Output: their lengths.
code.theory_link: A small dataset with 46 classes means overfitting will come quickly.

code.title: One newswire as a list of word indices
code.what_it_does: Prints the 11th training newswire as a sequence of 31 integer word indices.

line_explanations.explanation: 1 is the start-of-sequence marker; all other values are below 10,000 because of num_words. Repeated values (14, 26, 46, 61, 74, 4329) are repeated words.

code.inputs_outputs: Output: a Python list of 31 ints.
code.theory_link: Under multi-hot encoding the repetitions are lost: only which words occur matters, not how often or in what order.
pitfalls: The numbers are shifted by 3 relative to get_word_index(); see listing 4.12.

code.title: Decoding newswires back to text
code.original_code:
word_index = reuters.get_word_index()
reverse_word_index = dict([(value, key) for (key, value) in word_index.items()])
decoded_newswire = " ".join(
    [reverse_word_index.get(i - 3, "?") for i in train_data[10]]
)
code.what_it_does: Builds an index-to-word dictionary and uses it to turn train_data[10] back into a space-separated string.

line_explanations.explanation: get_word_index returns a dict mapping each word to its integer rank.
Inverts the dictionary so that integer keys map to words.

For each index i, look up i - 3. The callout explains that indices are offset by 3 because 0, 1 and 2 are reserved for 'padding', 'start of sequence' and 'unknown'. Missing keys give '?'. The words are joined with spaces.

code.inputs_outputs: Input: train_data[10]. Output: decoded_newswire, a str beginning with '?' (the start token).
code.algorithm: Dictionary inversion followed by per-token lookup with a default value.
code.theory_link: Integer tokenisation is reversible up to dropped rare words, which become '?' (out-of-vocabulary).

parameters.name: i - 3
parameters.role: Undoes the shift caused by the three reserved indices.
Placeholder for reserved or unknown indices.

pitfalls: Omitting '- 3' produces wrong words without raising any error.
get_word_index downloads a separate JSON file the first time it is called.
code.illustrative_code:
# AI-written: inspect the decoded text and label together
print(decoded_newswire)
print("topic:", train_labels[10])

code.title: A label is a topic index
code.what_it_does: Shows that the 11th newswire belongs to topic 3.

line_explanations.explanation: Labels are integers in 0-45; this one is 3.

code.theory_link: Integer categorical targets have to be one-hot encoded or used with a sparse loss.
pitfalls: Do not treat label values as ordered quantities.

deeper.title: Walking through the decoding of the first tokens
deeper.body:
For `train_data[10] = [1, 245, 273, ...]`:

1. `i = 1` gives `i - 3 = -2`, which is not a key, so `"?"`. This is the start-of-sequence token.
2. `i = 245` gives rank 242 in `word_index`, a fairly common word.
3. `i = 273` gives rank 270, and so on.

Any word that was outside the top 10,000 was replaced by the 'unknown' index 2 when loading, and also decodes to `"?"`. So the decoded text is the original wire with rare words masked and a leading `?`. (Walkthrough added; the specific decoded words are not printed in the book.)

deeper.title: Reserved seats
deeper.body: Think of a stadium where seats 0, 1 and 2 are always reserved (for padding, the 'start' flag and 'unknown visitor'). The ticket office's master list (`get_word_index`) numbers words from 1 by popularity, but when the words take their seats in the dataset everyone sits three places further along. To look someone up you subtract 3 from their seat number.

misconceptions.claim: The integers in train_data are word counts or frequencies.
misconceptions.correction: They are word indices (ids), ordered by frequency rank and shifted by 3; the sequence lists words in order.

misconceptions.claim: Labels 0-45 can be fed as a single numeric target to a regression output.
misconceptions.correction: They are category ids for 46 mutually exclusive topics; use a 46-way softmax with categorical or sparse categorical crossentropy.

misconceptions.claim: Reuters is as large as IMDb.
misconceptions.correction: It has only 8,982 training and 2,246 test examples, much less than IMDb's 25,000 + 25,000, and they are spread over 46 classes.

takeaways: reuters.load_data(num_words=10000) loads Reuters just like IMDb, keeping the 10,000 most frequent words.
There are 8,982 training and 2,246 test newswires, a small dataset for 46 classes.
Each newswire is a variable-length list of word indices; index 1 marks the start of the sequence.
Decoding needs an offset of 3 because indices 0, 1 and 2 are reserved for padding, start of sequence and unknown.
Labels are integer topic indices from 0 to 45, which will need categorical handling.

questions.question: How many training and test examples does the Reuters dataset have in Keras?
questions.explanation: Shown by len(train_data) and len(test_data). 25,000/25,000 is IMDb; 60,000/10,000 is MNIST; 10,000 is the vocabulary size and 46 the number of topics.

questions.question: Why does listing 4.12 look up i - 3 instead of i?
questions.answer: Because indices 0, 1 and 2 are reserved for padding, start of sequence and unknown, every stored word index is shifted by 3 relative to get_word_index().
questions.explanation: This is stated in the callout. Without the shift, every decoded word would be wrong.

questions.question: What does train_labels[10] = 3 tell you?
options: The newswire belongs to topic index 3 out of 0-45
The newswire is the 3rd in its topic
questions.answer: The newswire belongs to topic index 3 out of 0-45
questions.explanation: The page says the label is 'an integer between 0 and 45, a topic index'. It is not a count, a score or a position.

questions.question: train_data[10] contains the index 4329 twice. After multi-hot vectorisation into a 10,000-dimensional vector, what information about this word is kept and what is lost?
questions.answer: It is kept that the word occurs (position 4329 is set to 1). How many times it occurs and where in the text it appears are lost.
questions.explanation: Multi-hot encoding records only presence, as for IMDb (p.131).

questions.question: What effect does num_words=10000 have on what you see in train_data, and why is this useful?
questions.answer: Only the 10,000 most frequent words keep their indices; rarer ones are dropped (or mapped to the unknown index). This caps the input size at 10,000 dimensions and removes words too rare to help classification.
questions.explanation: Same reasoning as for IMDb on p.130.
